title: the sandals
hook: two brothers argue on a mountain, each trying to give the other a kingdom

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bharata's journey, part three. Guha suspected him, Bharadvaja questioned him, Lakshmana wanted to fight him, and Rama said: he comes in love. Did you say a sentence of trust? Day five hundred forty-eight.

On Chitrakoot, two brothers have an inheritance fight that runs backward: each one is trying to give the kingdom away. Bharata reaches the hut, sees Rama sitting in bark clothes with matted hair, and falls at his feet, unable to finish a sentence. Rama lifts him up, holds him, and asks the question Bharata has dreaded the whole road. Where is our father? Why have you left him to come here?
screen: `A FIGHT TO GIVE THINGS AWAY.` → `BHARATA AT RAMA'S FEET.` → `WHERE IS OUR FATHER?`

segments.voice: Bharata tells him. The king is dead, grieving for you. Rama falls like a cut tree. When he can stand, he goes down to the Mandakini with his brothers and Sita, and offers water to his father, and a ball of ingudi pulp, the forest food they've been living on. In Valmiki's telling, he says something tender about it: what a person eats, their ancestors eat too. Then the arguing begins, and it goes on and on. Bharata pleads: come home, be king, I'll serve you. The counselors and the priests plead. Rama's answer never changes. Our father gave his word to Kaikeyi, and made a promise to me. Keeping his word is how I honor him now. Fourteen years in the forest is my part. Ruling Ayodhya is yours. Bharata even threatens to sit fasting at the door of the hut until Rama gives in, and Rama gently tells him that isn't the way. Finally Bharata asks for one thing. He brings out a pair of sandals adorned with gold, and asks Rama to step into them, then give them to him. Rama puts his feet in them, steps out, and hands them over. Bharata bows to the sandals. For fourteen years, he says, these will rule. I'll live outside the city in bark and matted hair, waiting for you. And if you're not back on the first day after fourteen years end, I'll enter the fire. Neither brother wins the argument. Both keep their word.
screen: `WATER FOR A FATHER AT THE MANDAKINI.` · `COME HOME AND BE KING.` · `I KEEP MY FATHER'S WORD.` · `STEP INTO THESE SANDALS.` · then, large: `BOTH KEEP THEIR WORD.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Bring to mind one object that keeps someone present for you when they're away: a photo, a ring, a cup they gave you, a saved voice message. Picture it clearly, its color, its weight. Notice how a small thing can carry a whole person. Breathe slowly, and let that person be near for the length of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The sandals. Rama steps into a pair of gold-adorned sandals and gives them to Bharata, who will set them on the throne for fourteen years.
Your line: the sandals. Today, keep a promise someone else made on your behalf, even if it's small. Day five hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Rama's sandals, the padukas, are honored in Hindu worship and art, and Ramlila performances stage the brothers' meeting at Chitrakoot.

pairs: where Rama offers water to his father
the forest food offered to the ancestors

myth: Rama agrees to return after Bharata's pleading
he refuses every plea: keeping his father's word comes first.
Rama steps into the sandals before giving them
Bharata asks him to, then bows to them.
Bharata vows to enter fire if Rama is late
if Rama isn't back the day after fourteen years end.

fork.setup: you're Bharata. Rama won't come home, no matter what anyone says. what do you ask for?
options: his bow, as a sign of power.
his sandals, after he steps into them.
a written order making you king.
fork.reveal: he asks Rama to step into a pair of gold-adorned sandals, then carries them home to rule in Rama's name.

original.note: Sanskrit pādukā: a sandal or wooden shoe. Rama's pādukā are still honored in temples and homes.

trapdoor: what you thought: Bharata takes the sandals as a keepsake.
what it means: he takes them to place on the throne and rule in Rama's name.
what a scholar hears: Valmiki has Bharata ask Rama to step into the sandals first, so they carry his presence, and vow fire if Rama is late.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 99–103 (the meeting; the news; the offering at the Mandakini)
Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 104–112 (the pleas; Rama's refusal; the sandals)

notes: Jabali's argument and Rama's reply (Ayodhya 108–109) and Rama's long questions on kingship (Ayodhya 100) are left out for one idea; a Keeper may want them on a later day.
Rama's line that what a person eats, the ancestors eat too, is paraphrased; confirm.
Bharata's threat to fast at the door and the vow of fire are paraphrased; confirm.
'Bharat Milap' as a Ramlila episode: confirm naming.

Review (538–556 pass): cut the hook's 'most family fights' generalization; 'lasts for days' and 'the mothers plead' were not supported, now 'goes on and on' with counselors and priests (Jabali, Vasishtha); replaced the feet practice, which repeated day 540's bare-feet sit, with an object that keeps someone present; dropped the 'Bharat Milap' naming, which in Ramlila usually means the reunion after the exile.
